# Alfred North Whitehead Summary
Alfred North Whitehead (1861–1947) was a British mathematician and philosopher notable for his co-authorship (with Bertrand Russell) of *Principia Mathematica* , one of the 20th century's most influential works in mathematical logic, as well as his philosophical contributions to metaphysics and process philosophy. Educated at Trinity College, Cambridge, he taught mathematics there until 1910, then held positions at University College London, Imperial College London, and served in administrative roles in the University of London system, where he championed educational reform. Later, at Harvard University from 1924, Whitehead shifted his focus to philosophy, producing key works such as *Science and the Modern World* and *Process and Reality* . He emphasized the importance of imagination in education and opposed rote learning, advocating for transdisciplinary approaches and curriculum tailored to students' needs.
Whitehead's philosophical work introduced "process philosophy," which rejected substance-based metaphysics in favor of a view of reality as a constantly evolving network of interrelated events ("occasions of experience"). He argued for the primacy of relations over objects, with creativity as the universe's basic principle. Whitehead's ideas influenced fields ranging from theology (especially process theology) to ecology, education theory, and physics. His conception of God differed from traditional notions, describing God as relational, affected by and immanent within the world. Whitehead's legacy continues in specialized philosophical and theological circles, with ongoing influence in areas like ecological civilization and educational philosophy, especially in China and at select Western institutions. Among his major published works are *A Treatise on Universal Algebra* , *Principia Mathematica* , *An Introduction to Mathematics* , *Science and the Modern World* , *Process and Reality* , and *The Aims of Education and Other Essays* .
